01 / Profile

From mathematical models
to working systems.

I enjoy problems where the system is only partially observed, measurements are noisy, and the model must guide the algorithm.

I am currently pursuing an MSc in Systems & Control at Delft University of Technology. My academic interests centre on estimation, statistical signal processing, optimisation and the modelling of dynamic systems.

Across projects and research, I have worked with Kalman filtering, LQR/LQG, sensor fusion, physics-guided machine learning and image segmentation. Earlier industrial roles at Siemens and ABB gave me experience translating control logic into systems that can be tested and deployed.

I am especially drawn to research that connects mathematical reasoning with measurable physical outcomes — from extracting state information from sensors to computational methods for optical and imaging systems.

Selected technical work · Project notes

From model to measured behaviour.

A closer look at the modelling choices, implementation and results behind selected projects.

P / 01 · Optics · Estimation · Control

Adaptive Optics-Inspired Control

SIMULATION STUDY

Built a closed-loop optical simulation to study how slit disturbances affect focal-plane intensity, and compared PI, static interaction-matrix control and LQG-based disturbance compensation. The aim was to understand the trade-off between simple feedback, actuator dynamics and model-based prediction.

Optical setup and disturbance model

A monochromatic 633 nm HeNe plane wave passes through a mechanically disturbed slit. A thin lens with focal length 0.1 m performs a Fourier transform at the focal plane. The simulated focal-plane intensity follows a sinc-squared diffraction profile:

I(x,t) = [2a(t)/a₀]² · sinc²( a(t)[x − c(t)] / (λf) )

The slit width and centre are perturbed by sinusoidal disturbances at 2.0 Hz and 1.5 Hz, respectively, with additive noise. The controller uses ROI intensity and slit-centre information to compensate for these variations.

Controllers implemented

  • PI control: Proportional-integral feedback on slit position. The derivative term was excluded because it amplified measurement noise at the 1 ms simulation timestep.
  • Static D⁺ control: Identified a 2 × 2 interaction matrix by actuator poke testing and used its pseudoinverse to map sensor error to actuator correction. The matrix condition number was 7.48.
  • Actuator lag: Modelled first-order actuator dynamics with τ = 0.1 s (cutoff frequency approximately 1.6 Hz), close to the disturbance frequencies.
  • LQG: Identified disturbance frequencies using Welch’s PSD estimate, fitted a harmonic oscillator state-space model and used a steady-state Kalman filter to estimate and predict the disturbance for feedforward cancellation.

Quantitative results

ControllerMean ROIStd. dev.Comparison
Open loop0.12240.0186Baseline
PI0.12300.0037≈5× lower std.
D⁺, no lag0.12370.0004≈46× lower std.
D⁺, with lag0.12350.0147Lag-sensitive
LQG0.15010.0150Mean intensity recovered
What I learned: Static inverse control can perform exceptionally near its identification point, but actuator bandwidth and departures from the local linear regime matter. A disturbance model can improve compensation by predicting periodic motion, although the remaining variance is still constrained by actuator dynamics.
PythonFourier opticsWelch PSDPseudoinverseKalman filterLQG
P / 02 · Sensor fusion · State estimation

IMU-Based Orientation Estimation

REAL SENSOR DATA

Implemented and benchmarked classical attitude filters and learned sequence models on the TUM Visual-Inertial (TUM VI) dataset. The project focused on the complete estimation pipeline—from ROS bag extraction and quaternion kinematics to filter implementation, time alignment and evaluation against motion-capture ground truth.

Dataset and estimation methods

The calib-cam7 sequence was used. The IMU stream provides accelerometer and gyroscope measurements at 200 Hz; ground-truth orientation comes from the VRPN motion-capture transform topic. Stereo camera frames were extracted for completeness but were not used in the orientation estimates.

  • Classical filters: Madgwick and Mahony complementary-style filters, plus a custom quaternion EKF derived from the quaternion kinematic process model and numerically linearised measurement Jacobians.
  • Learned models: A two-layer Transformer encoder and an LSTM trained on 20-sample windows of nine-axis IMU data (accelerometer, gyroscope and magnetometer).
  • Evaluation: Roll, pitch and yaw RMSE in degrees after aligning estimates with ground-truth timestamps.

Results

MethodRoll RMSEPitch RMSEYaw RMSE
Transformer1.15°0.60°1.67°
LSTM1.40°1.32°2.74°
Madgwick2.48°2.51°1.97°
Mahony2.27°1.67°1.82°
EKF3.24°5.29°28.77°
Interpretation and limitations: The Transformer performed best on the evaluated sequence, but the learned models were trained and tested on the same calibration sequence; this does not establish generalisation to unseen trajectories. The EKF’s large yaw error points to magnetometer modelling, reference-frame assumptions or the numerical update Jacobian as debugging targets. Further work would include held-out-sequence evaluation, quaternion-aware loss functions and explicit sensor-bias estimation.

P / 05 · Renewable energy · Control

Wind Turbine Control & State Observer

DYNAMIC SIMULATION

Modelled a nonlinear two-mass wind-turbine drivetrain and implemented region-dependent torque and pitch control. The architecture switches between below-rated maximum-power-point tracking and above-rated pitch regulation, while monitoring drivetrain speed, shaft twist, torque, pitch angle and power.

Control architecture

Wind speed v(t) → Cₚ(λ, β) aerodynamic model → Tₐₑᵣₒ → rotor / drivetrain dynamics → ωᵣ(t)

ωᵣ < 0.9 ωᵣ,rated: MPPT, Tgen = Kopt · ωᵣ²
ωᵣ ≥ 0.9 ωᵣ,rated: PID pitch control → pitch actuator (rate limit ±8°/s)

The MPPT region follows the optimal torque-speed relationship. As rotor speed approaches rated speed, the controller transitions to pitch regulation, commanding blade pitch through a rate-limited actuator to constrain rotor speed and power. The model captures drivetrain flexibility and transient torsional response rather than treating the turbine as a single rigid inertia.

P / 08 · Industrial automation · ABB

HMI Upgradation for BALCO Narrow Cold Rolling Mills

INDUSTRY INTERNSHIP

As part of a third-year internship project at ABB, worked on the upgradation of the Human-Machine Interface (HMI) environment for BALCO (Bharat Aluminium Company Limited) narrow cold rolling mills. The project focused on transitioning the existing Wonderware-based HMI to ABB System 800xA, with the aim of improving process visualisation, operational reliability and integration with the plant’s existing control infrastructure.

Work carried out

  • Process familiarisation: Studied narrow cold rolling mill operations and the role of the HMI in monitoring process variables such as strip tension, rolling speed and equipment status.
  • Tag migration: Reviewed existing Wonderware tags, recreated and matched them in ABB 800xA, and validated data types and memory addressing.
  • Operator Workplace graphics: Developed static graphics and layout elements, including mill-stand visuals, equipment outlines and section labels. Linked dynamic objects to process tags for real-time monitoring and operator interaction.
  • System verification: Checked tag-to-object linkage, alarm handling and overall HMI functionality for consistency with the control infrastructure.

Tools and system context

The work involved ABB System 800xA Operator Workplace, Control Builder for control-logic configuration and the Import/Export Tool for system-data management. The report also examined communication between controllers, HMI stations and field devices, and discussed Level 2 automation concepts and OpenNMS-based network monitoring as supporting context.

Project outcome: The HMI migration and verification work supported a clearer operator interface and improved visibility of process information. The project provided practical exposure to industrial HMI engineering, tag management, alarm handling and the integration requirements of a live process-control environment.
